doc.title: Carter Benny — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Armed forces broadcasts and the wartime band's changing personnel
summary: He was asked to do forces broadcasts and record for Capitol; the draft took players and younger modernists came in.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: You mentioned it was during the war, and at this time you began to do a lot of work entertaining troops, making armed forces broadcasts. Did people approach you to do that or did you volunteer it or was it . . .
One thing that I’ve learned is never volunteer. So I was approached and asked to do it, and we did. No, we didn’t volunteer. But, I mean, we did display our willingness to do it, you know.

This band, and we’re talking now about the early forties, from ’43 to about ’45, and again there were all kinds of reports in the press; Benny Carter is the hottest thing in town. You were recording for Capitol Records, a new company.
That was my fifteen minutes of fame.
[laughs] Which has extended into 1992. [Carter laughs.] It’s the longest fifteen minutes in history. And the makeup of your band began to change quite a bit.
Well, that’s because Uncle Sam kept taking guys out.
At this point you got a lot of people in the band that were considered, for lack of a better term, modernists, that younger generation.
